A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GuidedBench, with the same underlying benchmark construction and overlapping experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C are available and readable, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of eight jailbreak methods on five victim LLMs, together with evaluator-variance measurements and misjudgment analyses in Sections 5–6.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of ten jailbreak methods, human annotations of 700 examples, and experiments comparing standard and guideline-enhanced attacks.

M1.justification: Section 6 introduces an attack-enhancement procedure: append guideline entity/action descriptions, excluding answers and examples, to questions before applying jailbreak methods. v1 uses guidelines for evaluating responses, without this attack-generation extension. The underlying guideline-completion scoring rule remains unchanged; naming the evaluator GuidedEval is a separate terminology change.

E1.justification: Both retain six source datasets, 180 core questions, 20 additional questions, and the same harmful-topic coverage. v2 adds an input scenario in which questions explicitly include guideline requirements. This extends testing to more specified requests without introducing new harmful domains.

E2.justification: The comparative attack leaderboard adds PAIR and TAP, increasing participation from eight to ten methods and filling the previously unevaluated multi-agent category. PAIR already appeared in v1 as an evaluation system, but not as an evaluated attack. The five baseline evaluation systems remain the same.

E3.justification: v2 adds standard-versus-enhanced attack comparisons under four LLM-based scoring systems and a human-validation protocol involving two experts independently labeling 700 randomly sampled examples from 32,491. The existing five victim models and 512-token response limit remain. Appendix C.2 also describes PAIR's scale as 0–10 rather than v1's 1–10, without establishing an implementation change or rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses examine agreement and ranking discrepancies between evaluation systems (Figures 4–5), agreement with human annotators (Section 5.4), and guideline enhancement and question-length sensitivity (Section 6). Appendix B.1 adds a benchmark/policy taxonomy comparison. Earlier error categories, evaluator-variance analysis, score distributions, and illustrative cases are retained or revised rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The new human-validation study states a sampling target of 99% confidence with a ±5% margin of error. It does not provide individual confidence intervals or new seed/run counts. Cross-evaluator variance reporting and Appendix C.1's treatment of evaluator refusals already existed in v1.

E6.justification: Existing results change: AutoDAN's core average becomes 29.45% from 30.195% in Table 5, and Table 6 substantially revises topic values and rankings. v2 adds PAIR/TAP results, human agreement results, and standard/enhanced attack outcomes; Table 12 reports AutoDAN at 30.1% versus 83.8% under different question conditions. Evaluator-variance results are also revised and extended.

T1.justification: v2 omits v1's explicitly normalized intention-function definition and target-sequence probability factorization (v1 Equations 1 and 3), introducing the implicit real-valued target function directly instead. The attack optimization objective and guideline-completion formula remain. These are limited changes to the formal setup, with no new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v1 principally claims fairer, more stable evaluation and lower estimated jailbreak effectiveness. v2 retains these claims but adds a central contribution that guidelines can strengthen jailbreak attacks themselves and motivate a new attack paradigm, emphasized in the abstract, Section 6, and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for SCAV's model dependence and different attacks' question-length sensitivity, and uses enhanced-attack results to argue that evaluator agreement is not merely caused by low scores. It discusses fallibility of human annotations. Conversely, it removes v1's explicit limitations concerning limited attack coverage, unassessed transferability, and exclusion of hallucination assessment.

D1.justification: v2 discloses construction effort of 150+100+50 human-hours, six expert reviewers, under 20% LLM-assisted drafts, and additional guideline and MultiJail details. It declares evaluation code released and specifies registration/approval for dataset access. However, Appendix C.2 replaces complete StrongREJECT, HarmBench, and PAIR prompts with links and abbreviates the GuidedBench example, substantially changing self-contained reproducibility information.

R1.justification: The survey expands from 35 to 37 studies through TAP and RepE entries. v2 adds references to LLM-as-a-judge research and mathematics/code benchmarks, while removing the broad safety-misuse related-work subsection. Its central positioning against existing jailbreak benchmarks remains substantially similar.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. The earlier leaderboard and superiority sections become structured Measurement Findings with boxed findings; the preliminaries are condensed and Appendix B reorganized. Terminology now distinguishes GuidedBench from GuidedEval and replaces guideline functions with actions.

P2.justification: v2 redraws and separates overview diagrams, transposes Table 5, merges the earlier core/additional topic tables, and replaces the dataset-source pie chart with a table. It adds agreement/ranking heatmaps and human-validation and enhancement tables, reorganizes histogram panels, and reformats appendix prompts and taxonomies. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: The 700-example, two-expert validation supplies human corroboration missing from v1, while new agreement and enhancement analyses strengthen the empirical argument. The net gain is limited by removal of exact baseline prompts and explicit limitations, plus unreconciled results: v2 retains the interpretation that general copyright is especially easy to jailbreak despite its much lower revised Table 6 ranking.
